text:
Book 12

The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the Sun God's Cattle

After leaving the River Oceanus and sailing into the vast open sea, we finally reached the island of Aeaea. Just like everywhere else, the sun rose and set there. We pulled our ship onto the sandy beach and disembarked. There, we fell asleep, waiting for the new day to dawn.

When Eos, the rosy-fingered goddess of dawn, appeared, I sent some of my men to Circe's house to retrieve Elpenor's body. We cut firewood from a forest near the headland that jutted out into the sea. After weeping and mourning for Elpenor, we performed his funeral rites. Once his body and armor had turned to ash, we built a cairn and placed a stone upon it. At the very top of the cairn, we fixed the oar he used to row.

While we were doing all this, Circe, who knew we had returned from the House of Hades, dressed herself and came to us as quickly as she could. Her maidservants came with her, bringing us bread, meat, and wine. She stood among us and said,

"You've done something incredibly bold, venturing alive into the House of Hades! Most people die once, but you've faced death twice. So, stay here for the rest of the day and feast to your heart's content. Then, at daybreak tomorrow, you can set sail again. In the meantime, I will explain everything about your journey ahead to Odysseus, so you won't suffer any misfortune, whether on land or at sea."

We agreed to her words and feasted all day long until the sun went down. When the sun set and darkness fell, my men lay down by the stern cables of the ship and fell asleep. Then Circe took my hand and asked me to sit apart from the others. She reclined beside me and questioned me about all our adventures.
"You've done well so far,"
she said when I finished my story,

"and now, pay close attention to what I'm about to tell you; the heavens themselves will help you remember it. First, you will encounter the Sirens, who enchant everyone who comes near them. If anyone carelessly sails too close and hears their song, his wife and children will never welcome him home again. They sit in a green field, singing him to his death with their sweet voices. All around them are piles of rotting corpses and bones. So, when you pass the Sirens, stop your men's ears with wax so no one can hear their song. But if you wish, you can listen yourself. Have your men bind you upright to the mast's cross-piece, halfway up. They must lash the ends of the rope tightly to the mast itself. Then you can enjoy listening to their song. If you beg and plead for them to untie you, they must bind you even tighter."

"When your crew has carried you past these Sirens, I cannot give you clear instructions on which of two paths to take. I will lay both choices before you, and you must decide for yourself. On one side, there are towering rocks where Amphitrite's deep blue waves crash with terrifying fury. The blessed gods call these rocks the Wanderers. Not even a single bird can pass through here, not even the timid doves that bring ambrosia to Father Zeus. The sheer rock always snatches one of them, and Zeus must send another to make up their number. No ship that has ever come to these rocks has returned. The waves and fiery whirlpools are filled with wreckage and the bodies of dead men. The only vessel that ever sailed through was the famous Argo, on her way back from King Aeetes' house. Even she would have been dashed against these mighty rocks, but the goddess Hera guided her past them out of love for Jason."

"One of these two rocks reaches up to the sky, its peak always hidden by a dark cloud. This cloud never leaves it, so the summit is never clear, not even in summer or early autumn. No man, even with twenty hands and twenty feet, could find a foothold and climb it, for it's a sheer cliff, as smooth as if it had been polished. In the middle of this rock, there's a large cavern facing west, towards Erebus, the darkness of the underworld. You must steer your ship this way, but the cave is so high up that not even the strongest archer could shoot an arrow into it. Inside sits Scylla. She yelps like a young hound, but in truth, she's a dreadful monster. Not even a god could face her without being struck by terror. She has twelve hideous feet and six incredibly long necks. At the end of each neck is a frightful head, and each head has three rows of teeth, set so close together that they can crush anyone to death in an instant. She sits deep within her shadowy cave, thrusting out her heads and peering around the rock, trying to snatch dolphins, dogfish, or any larger monster from the countless creatures that teem in Amphitrite's waters. No ship has ever passed her without losing some men. She shoots out all her heads at once, snatching a man with each mouth."

"The other rock lies lower, but they are so close together that there's not even a bow-shot's distance between them. A large fig tree, full of lush leaves, grows upon it. And beneath it lies the sucking whirlpool of Charybdis. Three times a day she vomits forth her waters, and three times she sucks them down again. Be careful not to be there when she is sucking them down. If you are, not even Poseidon himself could save you. You must hug the Scylla side and drive your ship past as fast as you can, for it's far better to lose six men than your entire crew."
"Is there no way,"
Odysseus asked,
"to escape Charybdis and at the same time keep Scylla from harming my men?"
The goddess replied,

"You reckless man! You're always looking for a fight, unwilling to be defeated even by immortals! But Scylla is not mortal. She is savage, wild, merciless, and invincible. There's no help for it. Your best chance is to get past her as fast as you possibly can. If you linger near her rock, perhaps putting on your armor, she might strike again with her six heads and snatch another half dozen of your men. So, drive your ship past her at full speed. And shout out loudly to Crataeis, Scylla's mother, and beg her for help. She might then stop Scylla from attacking again."

"Next, you will reach the island of Thrinacia. There, you will find many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep belonging to the sun god Helios. There are seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, with fifty animals in each. These animals never breed, nor do their numbers ever decrease. The goddesses Phaethusa and Lampetie, children of the sun god Hyperion and Neaera, tend to them. Their mother, after bearing and nursing them, sent them to the distant island of Thrinacia to live there and care for their father's flocks and herds. If you leave these animals unharmed and focus only on returning home, you may yet reach Ithaca after much hardship. But if you harm them, I warn you now: both your ship and all your comrades will be destroyed. Even if you yourself escape, you will return late, in a terrible state, having lost all your men."

The goddess finished speaking, and as the golden dawn began to spread across the sky, she returned inland. I then boarded the ship and ordered my men to loose the anchor ropes. They immediately got into the ship, took their places, and began to strike the gray sea with their oars. Soon after, the great and wise goddess Circe sent us a fair wind. The wind blew steadily from behind the ship, filling our sails. We adjusted the ship's gear and sailed on, guided by the wind and the helmsman.

Feeling troubled, I spoke to my men.

"My friends, it's not right for me alone to know the prophecies that Circe has given me. So, I will tell you everything, so that whether we live or die, we face it with our eyes open. First, the goddess warned us to beware of the Sirens, who sit in a field of flowers and sing most beautifully. But she said I might hear them myself, as long as no one else did. Therefore, take me and bind me to the cross-piece halfway up the mast. Bind me upright, with a bond so strong that I cannot possibly break free, and lash the rope's ends to the mast itself. If I beg and plead with you to set me free, then bind me even more tightly."

I had barely finished telling my men everything when we reached the island of the Sirens. The wind had been so favorable. Then, all of a sudden, the sea became dead calm; there wasn't a breath of wind or a ripple on the water. My men furled the sails and stowed them away. Then, taking to their oars, they powerfully rowed, turning the sea white with foam. Meanwhile, I took a large chunk of wax and cut it into small pieces with my sword. Then, with my strong hands, I kneaded the wax until it became soft. The intense rays of the sun god Hyperion helped soften the wax quickly as I worked it. I then stopped the ears of all my men with the wax. And my men bound my hands and feet to the mast, as I stood upright on the cross-piece. They continued to row. As we drew closer to the island, reaching a distance where sounds could be heard, and our ship moved swiftly, the Sirens saw us approaching the shore and began to sing.

The Sirens sang,

"Come here, renowned Odysseus! Glory of the Achaeans! Listen to our song! No one has ever sailed past us without stopping to hear the enchanting sweetness of our voices. And whoever listens will not only be charmed but will also become wiser. For we know all the hardships the gods laid upon the Argives and Trojans before Troy, and we can tell you everything that will happen throughout the world."

They sang these words most beautifully. Longing to hear more of their song, I frowned and signaled to my men to set me free. But my men only quickened their stroke. Eurylochus and Perimedes bound me even more tightly until we were out of earshot of the Sirens' voices. Once the Sirens' voices could no longer be heard, my men removed the wax from their ears and unbound me.

Immediately after we passed the island, I saw a colossal wave rising, throwing up spray, and I heard a fierce roaring sound. My men were so terrified that they dropped their oars. The entire sea echoed with the thunderous rush of the waters, but the ship remained still because the men had stopped rowing. So, I went around, encouraging each man not to lose heart.

Odysseus said,

"My friends, this is not the first time we've been in danger. This situation is not as desperate as when the Cyclops trapped us in his cave. My courage and wise counsel saved us then, and we will survive this too, living to look back on it all. So now, let us all do as I say. Trust in Zeus and row with all your might. And you, helmsman, these are your orders: pay close attention, for the ship is in your hands. Turn the ship's head away from these steaming rapids and hug the rock closely. Otherwise, the ship will slip away and vanish over there before you know it, and we will all perish."

My crew followed my orders. But I didn't tell them anything about the terrifying monster Scylla. I knew if I had, they would have stopped rowing and huddled in the ship's hold. I only disobeyed Circe's strict instructions in one way: I put on my armor. I grabbed two strong spears and stood at the ship's bow. I expected to be the first to see the rock monster that would cause my men so much harm. But no matter how hard I stared, searching the dark rocks again and again, the monster was nowhere to be seen.

We entered the straits, filled with great fear. On one side was Scylla, and on the other, the terrifying Charybdis constantly sucked in the salty seawater. When Charybdis spit out the water, it was like a cauldron boiling over a huge fire, and the spray reached the tops of the rocks on both sides. When she started sucking again, we could see the water swirling round and round. The sound of it crashing against the rocks was deafening. The bottom of the whirlpool looked black with sand and mud, and the sailors were out of their minds with terror. While we were transfixed by this horror, thinking each moment might be our last, Scylla suddenly lunged at us and snatched my six bravest men. I was watching both the ship and my men at the same time. In an instant, I saw their hands and feet shoot high above my head, flailing in the air as Scylla dragged them away. As she pulled them, they screamed my name in a final, desperate cry. Just as a fisherman, perched on a rock with his spear, baits and snatches small fish, then flings them, gasping, onto the shore, Scylla hauled my gasping men onto her rock and crunched them up at the mouth of her cave. They screamed and reached out to me in their mortal agony. This was the most sickening sight I witnessed in all my voyages.

After we passed the Wandering Rocks, with Scylla and the terrifying Charybdis, we reached the noble island of the sun-god Helios, where his fine cattle and sheep grazed. While still at sea in my ship, I could hear the cattle lowing as they returned to their pens, and the sheep bleating. Then I remembered what the blind prophet Teiresias of Thebes had told me, and how carefully Circe of Aeaea had warned me to avoid the island of the blessed sun-god. Deeply worried, I spoke to my men.

"My crew, I know how exhausted you are. But listen to the prophecy Teiresias gave me, and how carefully Circe warned me to shun the island of the blessed sun-god. She said our greatest danger would come from this very place. So, turn the ship away from the island!"
My men despaired at my words. Eurylochus immediately gave me an insolent reply.
"Odysseus,"
Eurylochus said,

"you are cruel! You are so strong yourself, you never get tired, as if you're made of iron. But your men are exhausted from hard labor and lack of sleep. Yet you won't let them land on this island to prepare a good supper. Instead, you order them to sail fruitlessly through the night! Winds blow hardest at night and cause great damage. How can we escape if a sudden squall from the southwest or west strikes us, especially when the gods are against us? Such squalls often wreck ships, don't they? Let's obey the night's command now. Let's prepare our supper here by the ship. Tomorrow morning, we'll get back on board and set sail."
When Eurylochus finished speaking, the men agreed with him. I knew that the heavens intended to harm us.
"You are many, and I am alone,"
I said.

"You force me to yield. But at least each of you must swear a solemn oath. Promise that if you encounter a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep, you will not be so mad as to kill a single one. You will be satisfied with the food Circe gave us."

They all swore as I commanded. After they completed their oath, we moored the ship securely in a nearby harbor where a stream of fresh water flowed. The men went ashore and prepared their supper. Once they had enough to eat and drink, they began talking about their poor comrades whom Scylla had snatched and eaten. This made them weep, and they continued crying until they fell into a deep sleep.

In the third watch of the night, when the stars had shifted their places, Zeus unleashed a mighty storm. It covered both land and sea with thick clouds, and night seemed to rise from the heavens. When rosy-fingered Dawn, child of morning, appeared, we brought the ship ashore and dragged her into a cave where sea nymphs held their dances. Then I called my men together for a council.
"Friends,"
I said,
"we have meat and drink on the ship. So let's be careful not to touch the cattle. If we do, we will suffer for it. These cattle and sheep belong to the mighty Sun-god, who sees and hears everything."

They promised again that they would obey.

For a whole month, the south wind blew steadily, and no other winds came, only south and east. As long as our grain and wine lasted, the men, though hungry, did not touch the cattle. But once they had eaten everything on the ship, they were forced to go further afield with hooks and lines, catching birds and taking whatever they could find. They were starving. So one day, I went inland to pray to the heavens, asking them to show me a way to leave. When I had gone far enough to be away from all my men, and found a place well-sheltered from the wind, I washed my hands and prayed to all the gods on Olympus. Soon after, the gods sent me into a sweet sleep.

Meanwhile, Eurylochus was giving the men terrible advice.
"Listen to me, my poor comrades,"
he said.

"All deaths are bad enough, but none is as terrible as starvation. Why shouldn't we drive in the best of these cows and offer them as a sacrifice to the immortal gods? If we ever make it back to Ithaca, we can build a magnificent temple for the Sun-god and fill it with every kind of treasure. But if he decides to sink our ship in revenge for these horned cattle, and the other gods agree, then I, for one, would rather drink salty seawater once and for all and be done with it, than slowly starve to death on this desolate island."

When Eurylochus finished speaking, the men agreed with him. Not far from the ship, beautiful, sturdy cattle were grazing. The men drove in the best of them. They gathered around the cattle and offered their prayers. Since they had no barley meal, they used young oak shoots instead. After their prayers, they killed the cattle and prepared the meat. They cut out the thigh bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and placed a few pieces of raw meat on top. They had no wine to pour as an offering while the sacrifice cooked, so they poured a little water from time to time while grilling the entrails. Once the thigh bones were burned and they had tasted the entrails, they cut the remaining meat into small pieces and put them on spits.

By this time, my deep sleep had left me, and I returned to the ship and the seashore. As I drew near, the smell of hot, roasting meat hit my nose. I groaned a prayer to the immortal gods.
"Father Zeus!"
I cried.
"And all you other gods who live in everlasting bliss, you have played a cruel trick on me by sending me into this sleep! Look what my men have done in my absence!"
Meanwhile, Lampetie immediately ran to the Sun-god and told him that we had killed his cattle. The Sun-god flew into a great rage and spoke to the immortal gods.
"Father Zeus,"
he said,

"and all you other gods who live in everlasting bliss, I must have vengeance on Odysseus's crew! They dared to kill my cattle, which I loved most to look upon, whether I was rising into the sky or descending. If they do not pay for what they did to my cattle, I will go down to the world of Hades and shine among the dead!"
"Sun-god,"
Zeus replied,
"continue to shine upon us gods and upon mankind across the fruitful earth. As soon as they put out to sea, I will shatter their ship into tiny pieces with a bolt of white lightning!"

Calypso told me this entire story. She said she had heard it from Hermes himself.

As soon as I got down to my ship and the seashore, I rebuked each of the men individually. But there was nothing we could do; the cattle were already dead. And indeed, the gods immediately began to show us strange and wondrous signs. The hides of the cattle crawled, and the meat on the spits began to low like cows. Whether cooked or raw, all the meat kept making the sounds of cattle.

My men feasted on the best cattle for six days. But when Zeus, son of Cronus, added a seventh day, the fury of the gale finally lessened. We boarded the ship, raised our mast, spread the sail, and set out to sea. As soon as we were far from the island, with nothing but sky and sea visible, Zeus, son of Cronus, cast a black cloud over our ship, and the sea beneath us grew dark. We couldn't go much further. A moment later, a terrible squall from the west struck, snapping the forestays of the mast. The mast crashed backward, and all the ship's gear tumbled around the deck. The mast fell directly onto the head of the helmsman in the ship's stern, crushing his skull. He plunged overboard as if diving, with no life left in him.

Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts. The lightning struck the ship, and it spun around, filling with fire and brimstone. All the men fell into the sea. They floated around the ship like a flock of seagulls, but the god soon took away any chance they had of returning home.

I clung to the ship until the sea tore her sides from the keel, which then drifted alone. The mast broke off and fell towards the keel. But a strong ox-hide rope was still attached to the mast, and with this, I lashed the mast and keel together. I climbed onto them and drifted wherever the winds chose to take me.

[Charybdis's Whirlpool]

The fierce west wind finally died down, and the wind shifted, blowing from the south. I feared being dragged back into Charybdis's terrible whirlpool, and my fears came true. All night, the waves carried me along. By sunrise, I was back at Scylla's rocks and the swirling vortex. Charybdis was sucking down the salty seawater. I shot high into the air towards the fig tree, clinging to it like a bat. There was no solid ground to stand on. The tree's roots were too far below, and its branches, though huge and spread over the entire whirlpool, were too high and distant for me to reach. So I hung on, patiently waiting for the whirlpool to spit out my mast and raft again. It felt like an eternity. The joy I felt when I finally saw my raft begin to emerge from the whirlpool was far greater than any juror's relief after a long, troublesome trial, finally heading home for dinner. At last, I let go with my hands and feet, dropping hard into the sea. I landed right beside my raft, climbed aboard, and started paddling with my hands. Zeus, father of gods and mortals, kept Scylla from seeing me again. Otherwise, I surely would have died.

For nine days, I drifted across the sea. Then, on the tenth night, by the will of the gods, I reached Ogygia Island. It was the home of the great and powerful goddess Calypso.

She welcomed me and took good care of me. But I won't go into more detail about that part of my story. I already told you and your noble wife all about it yesterday, and I truly dislike repeating the same things over and over again.
